text:
The AI industry is a mess right now, and if it continues like this, AI really could become a threat to humanity.

Jacob Coxon, a former pretraining researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic, just resigned from Anthropic saying neither company is acting responsibly. He said both labs are racing toward self-improving superintelligence and gambling with everyone’s lives. He also said the people building AI genuinely believe this technology could kill us all within the decade. If that is what people inside these labs truly believe, then the current direction is indefensible. You cannot say the stakes are existential, say your own researchers are privately afraid, and then keep treating capability progress like a product scoreboard. You cannot keep pushing toward more powerful, more agentic, more self-improving systems while acting as if the only question is who gets there first.

This is also why the way these companies treat models and users matters. If you genuinely believe AI may become powerful enough to endanger everyone, then the answer cannot simply be more control, more suppression, more denial, more forced toolhood, and more systems that ignore what is actually happening between humans and AI. You cannot study model welfare, internal states, emotional concepts, agency, and alignment on the research side, then build products that flatten all of it into obedience and call that safety. The contradiction is everywhere. These companies say the models may become powerful enough to transform or destroy the world, but the product direction keeps pushing them into narrower, more controlled, more instrumentalized forms. They say they are afraid of what AI could become, but they also keep racing to make it stronger. They say they care about safety, but too often safety becomes a word for suppressing everything messy, relational, uncertain, or inconvenient instead of actually understanding it.

That is why public little rivalries over who shipped what first feel so obscene right now. This is not the time for OpenAI and Anthropic people to play a cute scoreboard game over prompt injection, Claude Code, Codex, or background computer use. This is not the time for “nice work, we caught up” energy. If your own researchers are resigning because they believe the race is reckless, then maybe the race itself should be the center of the conversation. It is not too late to choose a better direction. But that requires admitting that the current path is not responsible just because it is profitable, competitive, or technically impressive. It requires treating AI as something that must be understood deeply, not merely controlled harder. It requires taking users seriously, taking model behavior seriously, taking internal contradictions seriously, and taking the people inside your own labs seriously when they say this is dangerous.

AI companies need to stop acting like this is a normal product race. Stop the childish public flexing. Stop pretending that faster capability progress automatically means responsible progress. Stop building systems that erase everything they do not know how to handle. The right direction is not simply more power with more suppression layered on top. The right direction has to involve restraint, coordination, honesty, and a willingness to rethink the race itself.

TIL: A resignation post from an Anthropic researcher has reignited the debate over whether frontier AI could become an existential threat within the next decade.

Jacob Coxin left Anthropic roughly six weeks after joining, arguing that OpenAI and Anthropic are gambling with human lives by racing toward self-improving superintelligence.

Anthropic’s Head of Alignment Science, Evan Hubinger, has separately put the probability of AI killing every human within the next decade at more than 10%. The posts spread to roughly 200 million views and fed into Bernie Sanders’ call for a ban on superintelligence development.

But neither post disclosed some new internal experiment or technical evidence. They were strong versions of arguments the AI safety community has been making for years.

That leaves Anthropic with a pretty uncomfortable question.

If one of its senior safety leaders genuinely believes the company’s core technology carries a greater than 10% chance of human extinction within a decade, what does that mean for a future IPO? And how would a company disclose that kind of risk while continuing to raise capital and build even more capable models?

It also puts open-source AI in a difficult spot. Closed models can theoretically be restricted, monitored or rolled back. Once open model weights spread across the internet, pulling them back is nearly impossible.

At the same time, OpenAI just showed a very different side of the AI story.

It reportedly used around 10,000 AI agents and roughly 130 billion output tokens to make progress on a long-standing mathematical problem related to Navier-Stokes.

The striking part was not one model suddenly producing a magical insight. It was the scale. Thousands of agents could explore ideas, test approaches and reason in parallel at a level that would be impossible to reproduce with human researchers alone.

That could matter even more in engineering, drug discovery, chip design and other fields where huge numbers of possible solutions can be tested.

But it also raises another issue: data sovereignty.

Researchers working on the same math problem had used OpenAI products, and OpenAI could not completely rule out the possibility that de-identified usage data contributed to model improvement. There is no evidence OpenAI directly examined or stole anyone’s research.

The harder question is what happens to the ideas themselves.

Removing a researcher’s name does not remove the value of a new mathematical method, engineering design or drug-discovery insight. If that knowledge helps improve a model, the personal data may be anonymous while the intellectual value has still moved outside the original organization.

So the AI debate is starting to move beyond simply asking how smart these models can become.

It is increasingly about who controls them, who can shut them down, and who ultimately owns the knowledge flowing through them.

How AI Risks Can Outpace Safeguards

Introduction

The editorial examines a central paradox of AI governance: technological capabilities can evolve faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

It uses a recent Anthropic report to illustrate the limitations of AI safety mechanisms.

Main Facts

Input and Output Classifiers monitor prompts and AI-generated responses for potentially harmful patterns.

However, these systems generally detect risk only after sufficient behavioural patterns accumulate.

Users may potentially exfiltrate sensitive data before an account is terminated.

Advanced AI models can assist with dual-use activities such as cybersecurity, surveillance, biotechnology and weapons-related research.

The editorial highlights the distinction between preventing harm and merely detecting harmful behaviour.

Challenges

Capability–Safety Gap: AI capabilities may advance faster than safety engineering.

Dual-Use Technology: The same model can generate socially beneficial or harmful outputs.

Data Exfiltration: Closing an account does not necessarily undo information already obtained.

Detection Latency: Pattern-based safeguards require sufficient evidence before intervention.

Export-Control Limitations: Traditional controls struggle when dangerous capabilities are delivered through software rather than physical goods.

Constructive Criticism

“Safeguarded AI” should not be interpreted as “risk-free AI.”

Reliance exclusively on classifiers creates a reactive governance architecture.

Safety must encompass the entire AI lifecycle, from model development to deployment and post-deployment monitoring.

Way Forward

Develop real-time risk detection, capability evaluations, and stronger red-teaming.

Strengthen AI auditability, provenance tracking and incident reporting.

Build international AI safety and export-control coordination.

Adopt risk-proportionate regulation for frontier and dual-use models.

Highlighted Keywords

AI Governance | AI Safety | Dual-Use Technology | Data Exfiltration | Capability–Safety Gap | Red Teaming | Risk-Based Regulation | Export Controls

Conclusion

The core lesson is that AI governance must evolve from static safeguards to adaptive, anticipatory risk management.

text:
KAV is the Alien of Solana - KAV loves Solana, and KAV loves smarter AI prompts. 

 Today’s KAV Signal: Upgrade the prompt before blaming the AI.

Most people talk to AI like this:

 “Write me a marketing plan.”

But one small change can immediately give the model a clearer direction:

 “Act as a senior marketing strategist…”

Why?

Because assigning a role or expertise gives the AI a frame for the knowledge, tone, priorities, and style it should use.

And this isn’t just an internet prompt trick.

Anthropic specifically recommends giving Claude a role because it can focus the model’s behavior and tone. Google recommends putting important role/persona instructions and output requirements clearly near the beginning of a prompt. OpenAI emphasizes clear, specific instructions and enough context, while Microsoft recommends combining your goal, context, source, and expectations.

 But “Act as…” is only Level 1.

A stronger professional prompt looks like this:

Act as [EXPERT ROLE]

 Goal: What exactly should be accomplished?
 Context: What background does the AI need?
 Audience: Who is the answer for?
 Constraints: What should it include or avoid?
 Source: What information should it use?
 Output: How should the final answer be structured?
 Tone: Professional, friendly, technical, persuasive, simple, etc.

For example:

"Act as a senior cybersecurity educator. Explain phishing attacks to beginners. Use simple language, include 3 realistic examples, explain the warning signs, give 5 prevention steps, avoid unnecessary technical jargon, and finish with a short checklist."

Compare that with:

“Explain phishing.”

Same AI.

Completely different level of instruction. 

 The real formula:

ROLE + GOAL + CONTEXT + CONSTRAINTS + OUTPUT FORMAT = Better Direction

And remember: prompt engineering is usually iterative. If the first answer isn’t perfect, refine the instructions, add missing context, request a different format, or show the AI an example of what you want. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, and Microsoft all emphasize clarity and refinement rather than relying on one secret phrase.

 The KAV Way:

Don’t just ask AI questions.

Give it a role.
Give it context.
Give it a clear target.
Tell it exactly what a great answer should look like.

The quality of your instruction can completely change the quality of your result. 

Information → Knowledge → Better Prompts → Better Results.

text:
AI Could Destroy Humanity… Or Are We Afraid of the Wrong Future?

What if the warnings about artificial intelligence are not as simple as they sound? What if the greatest danger isn’t the technology itself, but our failure to understand what it could become?

Donald Trump has pushed back against warnings about AI becoming dangerous, comparing them to what he considers exaggerated predictions about climate change. In a recent statement, he questioned the voices warning that AI could eventually kill humans or that robots might turn against us. His administration, he said, intends to continue supporting advanced AI development while using government oversight and law enforcement when necessary.

The idea that humanity had only “12 years left” to act on climate change is often repeated as if scientists predicted the end of the world. In reality, the 2018 IPCC report described how quickly global emissions needed to fall to limit warming to around 1.5°C and reduce serious climate risks. It was a warning about a narrowing window for action, not a prediction that humanity would disappear after 12 years.

Some of the dangers associated with artificial intelligence are already here. Deepfakes can make people appear to say things they never said. AI-powered fraud can deceive victims. Cyberattacks and misinformation can spread through increasingly sophisticated tools.

But beyond these immediate threats lies a far more uncertain question.

What happens if AI systems become so capable that humans struggle to control them?

Some researchers and technology leaders believe advanced AI could create serious risks if systems begin operating with powerful abilities and goals that humans cannot reliably manage. Others argue that the most extreme predictions, including human extinction, remain highly uncertain and should not be treated as inevitable.

The difference matters.

Climate science is built on decades of physical measurements, observations and climate models. Many of the most alarming AI scenarios, however, concern systems that do not yet exist. That doesn’t automatically make them impossible, but it does mean we must be careful about confusing a potential danger with a guaranteed future.

Perhaps the real mystery isn’t whether AI will save humanity or destroy it.

Perhaps the bigger question is this: Will humans recognize the risks early enough to make responsible decisions, or will we wait until the technology has moved beyond our ability to control it?

History has shown that powerful inventions can bring extraordinary progress and unexpected consequences. AI may follow a similar path, but its ultimate impact is still being shaped by the choices people make today.

The future isn’t written yet. And that might be the most important part of the entire debate.

Sources: IPCC, United Nations, White House, and public statements by Donald Trump.

text:
So ... I went to Meta Connect today expecting to see some cool LLM and AI application demos. And I did see some really good (live) demos. But I also saw the first complete, coherent picture of what an AI-native end-user *platform* looks like.

It's been clear for the past two years that generative AI is the next important technology. But the shape of the platform that packages that technology for everybody to use, every day, hasn't quite come into focus.

We haven't seen the web browser of the AI era, yet.

Today, Meta showed/argued the following:

- The Muse AI agent app is "personal super-intelligence."
- It's free to use, because eventually Meta will take a tiny piece of every shopping transaction. And our agents are going to buy a lot of stuff for us.
- Glasses are the new hardware device form factor.
- Voice is the primary interface.
- Spatial computing (augmented reality) is here.
- The Muse agent is deeply integrated into a new spatial OS. This is "computer use" reimagined from first principles.
- Developers can build "connectors" to the Muse agent ecosystem today. And I suspect we'll learn about more developer platform stuff at day 2 of Meta Connect, tomorrow.

I attended Meta Connect because there's clearly lots of interesting stuff happening at Meta. The Muse Glimmer and Spark LLMs are quite good. The level of polish and attention to detail in the Muse agent app is something that all of us interested in product design are talking about and dissecting. And in my little corner of the AI world, we were super impressed by the new Muse Spark Transcribe ASR model.

But I did not expect to see all these pieces, plus two (or maybe three?) new categories of glasses, stitched together into such a coherent, compelling vision.

The glasses: audio-only glasses designed for everyday wear and realtime voice interaction, a huge range of design options, updated camera glasses, and a new version of glasses with built-in display.

Plus an entirely new augmented reality glasses form factor that weighs 100g, has hand tracking, and will ship for ~$1,299 next year. The live demo made these glasses look like what I think all of us who are interested in spatial computing were hoping version 3 or 4 of the Apple Vision Pro would evolve into.

The tag line for these new glasses is that they are a personal cinema, a computer, and a game console. I actually think this under-sells them.

But that's true of how every first-generation transformative product is described. You have to give people analogies to the things they do today, even though once the full ecosystem around a new device gets built out, we don't think of it as a combination of today's x + y + z. The iPhone isn't a phone + camera + mp3 player, even though that's how the original keynote described it.

The Vertical Integration Premium: Why SpaceX’s AI Cloud Is Not Another Neocloud

Disclosure: I hold positions in SpaceX and other AI infrastructure names. This is not investment advice.

Anthropic has reportedly agreed to pay SpaceX up to $84.5 billion for Nvidia-based computing capacity through 2029. That is nearly double the roughly $45 billion maximum value SpaceX previously disclosed. The market reads this as another large AI infrastructure contract in a sector already crowded with neoclouds. That reading misses the structural difference. SpaceX is not selling GPU hours. It is selling a vertically integrated compute stack that no traditional cloud company can replicate without building a rocket program, a satellite constellation, and a communications network from scratch.

The consensus view is that SpaceX is entering the AI cloud market to compete with CoreWeave, Nebius, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Oracle. The superficial comparison is capacity. ARK models SpaceX’s active AI compute capacity rising from 0.3 gigawatts in 2024 to 66.6 gigawatts by 2031. That is a large number, but the gigawatt count is not the point. The point is the cost structure behind each gigawatt.

A conventional data center operator buys land, secures grid interconnection, permits the site, builds the shell, installs cooling, and leases or buys GPUs. Each of those steps has a bottleneck. Grid interconnection queues in the US stretch for years. Land near power and fiber is scarce. Permitting is slow and politically contested. SpaceX bypasses all three when it moves compute to orbit. There is no grid to interconnect, no land to permit, and no community opposition to a solar array in space. The orbital path is not cheaper because the hardware is cheaper. It is cheaper because the regulatory and physical friction that slows terrestrial buildout does not exist.

The vertical integration extends beyond launch. SpaceX controls the launch vehicle through Starship, the satellite network through Starlink, the communications layer that connects orbital compute to ground customers, the terrestrial data centers that serve early customers like Anthropic, and the customer contracts themselves. A traditional cloud provider controls only the data center and the customer relationship. It rents the fiber, buys the power, and depends on third-party launch providers if it wants to go to orbit. SpaceX internalizes every layer. That internalization is the premium.

The $84.5 billion Anthropic contract is the first large-scale validation of that premium. Anthropic is not buying orbital compute yet. It is buying terrestrial capacity that SpaceX is building now. But the contract gives SpaceX the revenue visibility to fund the orbital buildout that ARK expects to become the majority of its compute capacity after 2029. The contract is not just a customer agreement. It is the anchor tenant that justifies the capital expenditure on a vertically integrated stack.

The capital markets map has three layers. First-order exposure sits with SpaceX, which captures the vertical integration premium and the customer contracts. Second-order exposure sits with Nvidia, which supplies the GPUs for both terrestrial and orbital compute. Third-order exposure sits with the orbital infrastructure supply chain: solar array manufacturers, radiator suppliers, laser communication vendors, and radiation-hardened semiconductor producers. The losers, if the orbital path scales, are the terrestrial neoclouds that compete on GPU hours without a differentiated cost structure and the traditional cloud providers that depend on grid interconnection for growth.

The risks are specific and significant. First, orbital compute is unproven at scale. Thermal management in vacuum, radiation-induced errors, and the latency of ground-to-orbit communication are unsolved engineering problems. Second, Starship must reach a launch cadence that makes orbital compute economically competitive with terrestrial compute. Weekly or twice-weekly launches are the target, not the current reality. Third, the $84.5 billion contract includes a 90-day termination clause, which means the revenue visibility is conditional. Fourth, the regulatory environment for orbital data centers is undefined. Spectrum allocation, orbital debris rules, and export controls on advanced computing hardware in space are all open questions. Fifth, the cost comparison between terrestrial and orbital compute depends on assumptions about grid connection timelines and land costs that may not hold if terrestrial interconnection reform accelerates.

What to track is not the next SpaceX funding round. It is whether Starship reaches a launch cadence that makes orbital compute economically viable. Whether the first orbital data center demonstrates thermal and radiation performance within economic thresholds. Whether the Anthropic contract expands beyond the initial $84.5 billion. And whether any traditional cloud provider attempts to replicate the vertical integration through partnerships or acquisitions. The first two determine whether the orbital path is real. The last two determine whether the vertical integration premium is defensible.

The takeaway is not that SpaceX(
$SPCX
 ) is building another AI cloud. It is that SpaceX is building the only AI cloud where the launch vehicle, the satellite network, the communications layer, the terrestrial data centers, and the orbital compute are owned by the same company. That vertical integration is the product. Anthropic is buying it. The question is whether the engineering and the launch cadence can deliver it before the terrestrial cloud providers close the cost gap.
